 Steve Smith lost the captaincy after the 2018 ball tampering scandal. Will its re-emergence see him travel full circle? Photograph: Robbie Stephenson/PA View image in fullscreen Steve Smith lost the captaincy after the 2018 ball tampering scandal. Will its re-emergence see him travel full circle? Photograph: Robbie Stephenson/PA Sportblog Australian ball tampering Steve Smith’s silence speaks louder than words to reshape his sandpapergate legacy
 Martin Pegan The wheel has turned in a way nobody could have scripted eight years ago with Australia’s former Test captain in the frame to take back the reins
 Fri 20 Nov 2026 09.00 EST Last modified on Fri 20 Nov 2026 11.31 EST Share Australian cricket is back talking itself into circles around “sandpapergate” more than eight years after a ball tampering agent was taken on to the field in Cape Town.
 Usman Khawaja’s autobiography, David Warner’s continued commentary, Pat Cummins’ 68-minute press conference and Cameron Bancroft’s 4,000-word first-person account have added fuel to the fire that has engulfed Australian cricket all over again. But there is one voice we are yet to hear from, and his silence is speaking louder than words.
 Steve Smith was as central to the story as anyone when Bancroft was filmed handling sandpaper on the field at Newlands during the third Test against South Africa in 2018. His insistence on fronting the media in the aftermath, which Bancroft said this week was done with an expectation that “owning up to the incident would help contain the damage and allow us to move forward”, instead ensured his place as one of the drama’s main characters.
 Sandpapergate has gone from a sporting scandal to a rolling loop of outrage and overreaction | Jonathan Horn Read more Images of a shell-shocked Smith’s walk of shame at Johannesburg airport a few days later, then of him breaking down in tears as he spoke to media after landing in Sydney, are among the most enduring from the time outside Bancroft stuffing part of a carpentry tool down his cricket trousers.
 The Australian captain at the time, like Bancroft and his vice-captain Warner, paid what is now widely considered to have been a disproportionate price. A 12-month suspension and a two-year leadership ban were the immediate costs. But these sanctions have paled in comparison to the stigma that has been attached to Smith since then for his role in the ball tampering saga.
 While several of Smith’s teammates and coaches from that notorious tour have picked their sides in the debate and taken aim at each other with varying degrees of venom and subtlety, the leader of Australia’s dressing room eight years ago has stayed out of the crossfire.
 Keeping his own counsel since returning from the playing ban, and especially in recent weeks, has inadvertently painted Smith in a more positive light. It may just be the biggest step he has taken in earning back respect, and a fair dose of public sympathy, since being banned by Cricket Australia in 2018 for his failure of leadership.
 Bancroft’s essay published this week has turned the blowtorch on Cummins with an emotional account of how he felt “angry, betrayed and alone” while watching the current Australia captain deny any knowledge of the ball tampering plot. His written account reinforced another image that has followed Smith through his career: a batter so absorbed in his technique, his method and his craft that he has treated everything away from the crease as a distraction.
 View image in fullscreen Smith breaks down in a media conference after being sent home from South Africa following the ball tampering scandal in 2018. Photograph: Steve Christo/AP Bancroft said when the sandpaper plan was floated in Port Elizabeth, Smith entered the conversation and made it clear that “he wanted no part in it before distancing himself”. When sandpaper was having the desired effect during the second Test, Smith dodged the discussion with the line that must still make his skin crawl: “I don’t want to know about it.”
 An ability to block the outside noise is part of what has made Smith one of Australia’s batting greats with more than 11,000 runs and 37 centuries across 127 Tests. “Steve just wanted to clear it so he could focus on batting,” Bancroft recalled as to why his captain wanted to press ahead with a media conference when they were being advised to wait.
 View image in fullscreen Smith’s silence during the resurgent sandpaper scandal could define his legacy. Photograph: William West/AFP/Getty Images Smith’s single-mindedness is shown in the repetitive rituals that mark his time in the middle. The shadow batting, the practice swings, the tugs at a glove and brushing of a pad while waiting for the bowler to start their approach have become as identifiable as Smith stepping across his stumps or raising his bat to celebrate another ton.

 This same mentality was part of his downfall in 2018 as he was banned and forced to hand over the captaincy, but now it could be the key to him going full circle in the twilight of his career.
 The 37-year-old is fairly presumed to be in the early days – or perhaps further along – of his farewell tour. Smith has consistently refused to state when his time with the national team might end, but two high-stakes Test series in India and England, which will follow a home summer against New Zealand, must be hard to resist for a player who has tasted great success but never been part of an Australia squad winning away to their biggest rivals.
 An outsider’s view of Australian cricket’s civil war: conflicting ‘truths’ and Cummins in a corner | Ali Martin Read more As pressure mounts on Cummins over whether he can hold on to the captaincy while his and Australia’s most senior bowlers stand firm on their position that they were not aware of the sandpaper plot in Cape Town, Smith remains off to the side, batting in the shadows.
 Smith has maintained his silence even after returning from his home away from home in New York to prepare for the summer’s four Tests with a Sheffield Shield hit-out with New South Wales this weekend.
 The silence will have to come to an end soon, but the longer Smith keeps his own counsel, the more it feels like his sandpapergate legacy is being reshaped to put the player who just wants to bat back in the frame to reclaim the reins of the Test team.
